comparisons.interpretation: Lewis George emphasizes tenant protections, deeper affordability and expanded public investment; Todd emphasizes housing delivery and funding already secured. Both discuss the Housing Production Trust Fund positively, so the evidence does not support a simple pro-/anti-public-housing split.

Both favor violence-interruption programs. Lewis George gives Cure the Streets immediate priority; Todd combines interruption funding with police and other measures. Lewis George's non-answer to the vice-squad portion is not opposition.
Lewis George names free bus-rail transfers; Todd names fare-free Circulator service and WMATA fare subsidies. These affect different service and fare structures and can coexist.

Lewis George emphasizes independence from corporate/developer donors and accountability; Todd emphasizes experience and working relationships inside government. Neither campaign's claims about the other's motives or record are treated as verified facts.

Lewis George outlines a broad tenant-protection and public-investment program; Edwards emphasizes replicating a particular affordable-development model at Walter Reed. No unsupported comparison between household-income and AMI thresholds is made.

Lewis George foregrounds trained civilian violence interrupters; Edwards foregrounds community policing, patrols and police-school relationships. This is a contrast in proposed interventions, not an inferred categorical rejection of all other safety measures.
Lewis George emphasizes donor independence and challenging insiders; Edwards emphasizes service navigation and cross-agency coalition experience.
Both explicitly support single payer through the New York Health Act. Mays-Williams's support must not be inferred away from her former-prosecutor background or her separate parole qualifications.
Both support co-sponsoring Good Cause Eviction protections. Mays-Williams's short affirmative is bound to the specific preceding question.
Both prefer ending421a. Alexis separately describes stronger conditions as a fallback if repeal cannot pass; the shared preferred position does not erase that legislative qualification.

Alexis commits to co-sponsoring Fair and Timely Parole; Mays-Williams is unsure about the bill as written and seeks amendments. Her qualified answer is not categorical opposition to parole or rehabilitation.

Alexis organizes his lead priorities around housing, healthcare and climate; Mays-Williams around gun-violence prevention, childcare and food security. Their policy overlap, including healthcare and tenant protections, remains explicit.
Both favor full sex-work decriminalization and oppose the Nordic model in their own explanatory answers.
